title: Supreme (Sn 4.5)
hook: read it: calling your own view best
tomorrow: what's still yours from a dream, once you wake up?

segments.voice: Yesterday, pure: not made pure by grabbing a view or a rite; the monkey can rest on one branch. Not by views. Then a question: what does calling your view the best cost?

The men are hitting each other now. Fists, shoving, shouting over one another. It's a pot! It's a post! It's a broom, you fool! A king watches, and he's delighted, because he set this up. He had men who were born blind brought to an elephant, each one placed at a different part, and then asked each: what is an elephant like? So that's the cost of calling your view the best. Not just being wrong. The fistfight.
screen: `IT'S A POT! IT'S A POST!` → `A KING SET THIS UP.` → `THE COST: THE FISTFIGHT.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Udana, and the Buddha tells it about teachers of his day who argued, this alone is true, everything else is worthless. The man at the head said a pot. The ear, a winnowing basket. The leg, a post. The tail, a pestle. Each one touched something real. The fight began when one part was called the whole. The fifth poem of the chapter of eights says the same thing without the elephant. In paraphrase from the Sutta Nipata: a person who settles into a view and calls it the highest in the world will call every other view inferior, and so never gets past quarrels. The skilled call that a knot. Then the poem turns the light on the one doing the measuring. Don't think of yourself as equal, it says, or lower, or better. Hear that again. Not only don't think you're better. Don't think you're worse, either, or exactly even. Drop the scale. And among people who are divided, don't take a side just to have one. Not the best isn't false modesty. It's putting the ruler down.
screen: `THIS ALONE IS TRUE, THEY ARGUE.` · `ONE PART CALLED THE WHOLE.` · `NOT EQUAL, NOT LOWER, NOT BETTER.` · `PUT THE RULER DOWN.` · then, large: `NOT THE BEST.`

segments.voice: Look at one object near you, a mug, a shoe, a pillow. Notice how much of it you can't see from where you are: the bottom, the inside, the far side. Turn it slowly in your hands, or in your mind, and let each new side count as part of the same thing.
Supreme: the highest. The poem's warning is about calling your own view supreme, which turns every other view into something lower, and you into a fighter.
Your line: not the best. Not the worst, either; just one side of the elephant. That's poem five.

howItsDone: The parable of the blind men and the elephant is told in Buddhist teaching on clinging to views, and versions of it are also told in other Indian traditions; the chapter of eights is studied for its teaching on letting go of views.

original.note: Pali: highest, supreme. The poem is the Paramaṭṭhaka Sutta, the eight verses on the supreme.

sources.ref: Udana 6.4 (Tittha Sutta: the blind men and the elephant)

notes: Udana 6.4 paraphrased: the king has men born blind shown an elephant; head = pot, ear = winnowing basket, leg = post, tail = pestle (the sutta lists more parts); they quarrel and strike each other with fists; the king is delighted; the Buddha applies it to quarreling sectarians. Confirm details.

Sn 4.5 paraphrased: one who dwells in views, making them highest, calls all others inferior and so has not gone beyond disputes; the skilled call this a knot; one should not consider oneself equal, inferior or superior; does not take sides among those divided. Confirm.
